title:
Discovering Underpotentially
Deposited Crystalline
Sodium Metal Nanoparticles on the Surface of Hard Carbon Anodes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sodium-ion batteries are attractive candidates for low-cost and scalable energy storage in which hard carbon (HC) anodes are used. However, sodium (Na) metal plating in HC anodes at voltages above the plating potential remains a critical problem. The location and spatial distribution of crystalline sodium (c-Na) metal nanoparticles, the clusters associated with Na storage in HCs, are important for understanding this underpotential plating behavior but remain unclear. Here, we implement a cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and electron tomography (cryo-ET) workflow that directly localizes c-Na metal clusters in sodiated HC samples: cryo-ET maps nanoscale three-dimensional (3D) distributions, while cryo-EM resolves local structure and chemistry. Our workflow reveals that c-Na metal clusters reside predominantly on the surfaces or near surfaces of individual HC particles. This finding challenges existing interpretations in the literature that locate the c-Na metal clusters within closed nanopores in the bulk of the HC, presumably because prior characterization using nonimaging techniques and two-dimensional (2D) projection images associated with traditional transmission electron microscopy (TEM) lacks the spatial 3D information necessary to resolve the full spatial distribution. Our discovery is an important step toward explaining the underpotential plating phenomenon of Na metal in HC anodes, suggesting that particle-level surface and near-surface interfaces are relevant targets to mitigate plating alongside bulk-pore, electrode, and electrolyte/interphase design.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society
summary: Cryo-ET combined with cryo-EM localizes crystalline Na metal clusters in sodiated hard carbon in 3D. They sit on or near particle surfaces, not in closed bulk nanopores as commonly assumed. This changes the picture of underpotential Na plating and points to surface and interface mitigation.

title: Diagnosing the Role of Mn Additives in Aqueous Zn/MnO2 Batteries
content:
Aqueous zinc‐ion batteries frequently employ manganese dioxide cathodes and prevent capacity fade with manganese electrolyte additives. Using operando X‐ray fluorescence spectroscopy to directly track Mn concentration during cycling, we show that the beneficial role of the Mn additive appears to be as an additional source of redox‐active material, rather than acting to suppress cathode dissolution.








ABSTRACT
Manganese dioxides are pervasive as cathode materials for aqueous zinc‐ion batteries; however, their energy storage mechanism has proven to be complex. Increasing evidence suggests that Mn dissolution contributes to cathode capacity via a reversible dissolution‐redeposition process, in addition to capacity from Zn2+/H+ (de)intercalation. Understanding the role played by Mn2+ in the electrolyte, particularly when introduced as an electrolyte additive, is important for diagnosing cathode degradation. Using operando X‐ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy, we track Mn2+ in operating cells to gain insights into the complexity of the MnO2 cathode. While some suppression of cathode dissolution by the additive cannot be excluded, our measurements suggest that Mn2+ electrolyte additives improve cycling performance by supplying extra redox‐active Mn during charge, rather than solely by suppressing Mn dissolution, thereby compensating for cathode degradation. Benefiting from operando XRF, we propose that a potential contributor to capacity fading is the incomplete dissolution of the MnO2 cathode and incomplete redeposition of Mn2+ from the electrolyte, and that this fading does not appear to be mitigated by using Mn2+ additives. These findings underscore the necessity of directly tracking Mn2+ evolution, and that improving reversibility requires addressing both the dissolution of MnO2 and the redeposition of Mn2+.
journal: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
summary: Operando XRF directly tracks electrolyte Mn2+ concentration during cycling of Zn/MnO2 cells. It suggests the Mn additive works mainly as extra redox-active Mn rather than by suppressing dissolution. It also points to incomplete MnO2 dissolution and Mn2+ redeposition as a cause of fade, which the additive does not fix.

title: Operando Mapping of Population Phase Separation and Lithium‐Plating Dynamics in Graphite Electrode Using Optical Microscopy and Microstructure Modeling
content:
Operando optical microscopy and three‐dimensional phase‐field modeling reveal how interfacial reaction kinetics and particle microstructure govern phase separation and lithium plating in graphite electrodes. A new interfacial‐ohmic‐resistance plating mechanism emerges before surface saturation. Particle‐size‐distribution design and thermal activation suppress lithium nucleation, growth, and concentration gradients, offering physics‐based strategies for safe fast charging.








ABSTRACT
The fast‐charging capability of phase‐separating graphite electrodes is largely constrained by heterogeneous reaction kinetics and sluggish mass transport at both the particle and electrode scales, which increase the risk of parasitic lithium plating and associated safety concerns. A deeper mechanistic understanding of the interplay among phase‐separation dynamics, electrode microstructure, and lithium‐plating propensity is therefore essential for guiding the rational design of advanced electrode architectures and fast‐charging protocols. Here, we combine operando optical microscopy with three‐dimensional microstructure‐resolved phase‐field modeling to resolve the interplay between phase separation and lithium plating. Microscopy captures stages evolution, phase mode transitions and structural dynamics across the particle population and at the single‐particle level, which is driven by the slow interfacial reactions. Non‐equilibrium phase‐field simulations elucidate the kinetic control mechanisms governing phase transitions as the current varies. Importantly, a new mechanism of lithium plating associated with interfacial ohmic resistance is identified. Based on these insights, we evaluate particle‐size‐distribution design and use thermal activation as a mechanistic probe to resolve how temperature alters phase‐separation pathways and lithium‐plating behavior. These results may serve as a foundation for improving the physical understanding and driving optimization of fast charging protocols for lithium‐ion batteries.
journal: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
summary: Combines operando optical microscopy of graphite staging across the particle population with microstructure-resolved phase-field simulation. It proposes a plating mechanism driven by interfacial ohmic resistance that sets in before surface saturation. It also uses particle-size distribution and temperature as probes of phase-separation pathways and plating onset.

title: Operando X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy Reveals Oxide Solid Electrolyte Stability against Electrochemically Plated Lithium
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) has revealed many possible Li-induced interfacial reactions in solid-state electrolytes (SSEs), but most in situ studies form Li|electrolyte interfaces through non-electrochemical Li deposition, including evaporation, sputtering, or electron-beam-induced deposition. These routes may introduce additional energy that activates reaction pathways not accessed during electrochemical Li plating. Here, we use lab-based operando XPS to directly evaluate oxide solid-state electrolyte stability during electrochemical Li formation. Using this approach, we find sharply different responses for two representative oxide SSEs: NASICON-type Li1+xAlxTi2–x(PO4)3 (LATP) is reduced upon Li plating, forming a Li+/Ti3+-rich mixed-conducting interphase that partially relaxes through coupled ionic–electronic redistribution, whereas garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) shows no spectroscopically resolvable Zr or La reduction. This work represents the first direct operando XPS evaluation of SSE stability against electrochemically plated Li metal.</jats:p>
summary: Electrochemical Li plating inside the XPS avoids the artefacts of evaporated or sputtered Li. LATP is reduced to a Li+/Ti3+ mixed-conducting interphase that partly relaxes, while LLZO shows no resolvable Zr or La reduction. This is a clean, direct test of the thermodynamic-instability predictions. It is spectroscopy, not spatially resolved imaging.
technique: lab-based operando XPS during electrochemical Li plating

title:
Mechanistic Insights
of Jahn–Teller Effect
Suppression in High-Entropy Prussian Blue Analogue Cathodes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Jahn–Teller (J-T) effect, as discovered by Hermann Jahn and Edward Teller in 1937, often causes lattice distortion and structural instability in Mn-based battery materials. Recent studies suggest that high-entropy design may help suppress J-T distortion, yet the underlying mechanism remains largely elusive due to their compositional complexity and structural disorder. Herein, using a Mn-based Prussian blue analogue as a case study, we employed a machine learning interatomic potential combined with synchrotron extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy (EXAFS) to elucidate the fundamental mechanism of the J-T suppression in high-entropy materials. Unexpectedly, EXAFS spectra reveal the absence of the typical J-T Mn–N bond-length splitting in our high-entropy Prussian blue analogue sample, but instead a broader Mn–N bond-length distribution. Machine learning-assisted calculations demonstrate the [MnN6] octahedra exhibit randomly oriented distortions along x-, y-, and z-axes in high-entropy lattices, resulting in the local distortion averaging out at the macroscopic scale. Further analysis of the local Mn coordination environment reveals that the high-entropy configuration enhances d-electron delocalization and reduces the energy splitting between Mn dx2–y2 and dz2 orbitals. This allows two structurally and electronically distinct distortion modes to coexist within the lattice, which disrupts long-range cooperative J-T order. Strikingly, the ultralong cycling stability of high-entropy K0.46[Mn0.21Co0.19Ni0.21Cu0.20Zn0.19][Fe(CN)6]0.98·1.69H2O is experimentally demonstrated, achieving 91.0% capacity retention over 50,000 cycles for aqueous ammonium-ion storage, which surpasses all of the Mn-based rechargeable batteries to date. Our study uncovers the microscopic mechanism of J-T suppression in high-entropy materials and provides an effective strategy for designing durable high-entropy battery electrodes.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society
summary: EXAFS shows no Mn–N bond-length splitting in a high-entropy PBA, only a broader distribution. MLIP calculations explain this as randomly oriented [MnN6] distortions along x, y and z that average out and break cooperative J-T order. The paper links this mechanism to 91% capacity retention over 50,000 cycles. It is local-structure work, not imaging.

title:
Vacancy-Induced
Ligand-Hole Character Redirects Oxygen
Redox in Li-Rich Layered Oxides
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Li-rich layered oxides access high capacities through the combined participation of transition-metal and oxygen redox, but oxygen oxidation is often coupled with irreversible structural rearrangement and voltage decay. Here, we show that oxygen-vacancy-preconditioning modifies the local Ni–O electronic structure and promotes oxygen-derived ligand-hole character in a Li-rich layered oxide. High-temperature quasi-single-crystal (QSC) formation generates oxygen-deficient local environments while preserving the overall layered framework. Synchrotron spectroscopy combined with density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveals enhanced Ni–O hybridization and redistribution of charge compensation toward oxygen-derived states. Mapping resonant inelastic X-ray scattering further shows earlier oxygen participation during charging, followed by increased delocalization of oxygen-derived holes within hybridized transition-metal–oxygen states. This modified redox pathway suppresses Mn reduction and is coupled to a distinct structural response in which transient lattice environments formed during the initial cycle progressively relax during prolonged cycling, while the layered framework is largely retained. The resulting cathode exhibits reduced voltage hysteresis and voltage decay, together with improved electrochemical reversibility. These results establish a direct connection between vacancy-modified ligand-hole character and oxygen-redox-driven structural relaxation, demonstrating how local electronic structure governs the structural pathway of oxygen-redox-active layered oxides.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society
summary: Oxygen-vacancy preconditioning in quasi-single-crystal Li-rich oxide is linked, via mapping RIXS, to earlier oxygen participation and more delocalised O holes in hybridised Ni–O states. This suppresses Mn reduction and voltage decay. The spectroscopy is solid, but it is bulk-averaged and not spatially resolved, and the work is still a material-modification study.
technique: mapping RIXS (mRIXS), soft X-ray absorption, DFT

title:
Mechanistic Insights
into Sodium Storage in N-Doped
Graphene/MoS2 Heterostructures Revealed by Operando Raman
Spectroscopy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Two-dimensional (2D) heterostructures offer tunable interlayer spacing and accessible surfaces that can overcome key limitations of conventional sodium-ion battery (SIBs) anodes. Here, we investigate Na+ storage mechanisms in three-layer 2D heterostructures composed of horizontally stacked graphene (G), nitrogen-doped graphene (NG), and MoS2 (M) by combining cyclic voltammetry with operando spectroelectrochemical Raman spectroscopy. Restricting the active thickness to three atomic layers enables direct spectroscopic access to interfacial charge transfer and strain during cycling. Electrochemical analysis reveals that Na+ storage is governed by two coupled factors: the permeability of the electrolyte-facing outer layer, and the electronic–mechanical interactions within the interlayer space. NG outer layers facilitate ion access and deliver up to 40-fold higher capacities than pristine graphene stacks, whereas MoS2 top layers suppress ion infiltration. Operando Raman correlates faradaic features with reversible structural changes, allowing separation of charge-doping and strain effects during cycling. The results demonstrate that Na+ storage proceeds predominantly via reversible accumulation in confined interlayer and blister-like reservoirs formed during solvent cointercalation. Incorporating MoS2 as a middle layer redistributes charge and buffers mechanical strain, enhancing cycling stability. These findings provide insights into charge storage mechanisms in 2D materials.</jats:p>
summary: Uses three-atomic-layer G/NG/MoS2 stacks so operando Raman can separate charge-doping from strain during Na+ cycling. Concludes storage is mainly reversible accumulation in interlayer and blister-like reservoirs formed by solvent cointercalation. The outer layer controls ion access: N-doped graphene gives up to 40× the capacity of pristine graphene, and MoS2 on top blocks infiltration.

title:
Watching Electrochemical
Interfaces in Motion with
High-Speed Atomic Force Microscopy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrochemical processes involve transient phenomena, including nucleation and growth, phase transformations, dissolution, ion transport, and interfacial restructuring, which are difficult to capture simultaneously at nanoscale and in real time under electrochemical controls. High-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM), originally developed for dynamic biological imaging, combines nanometer-scale spatial resolution with frame times of approximately 0.1–5 s/frame, extending into the subsecond regime, enabling direct visualization of electrochemical interfaces under operando conditions. This perspective highlights emerging applications of HS-AFM in electrochemistry, including electrodeposition, nanoparticle dissolution, corrosion, lithiation-induced morphological evolution, protein adsorption, and nanobubble dynamics. HS-AFM reveals that mechanistic insight often resides in transient, nonequilibrium pathways rather than equilibrium structures alone. Advances will enable real-time nanoscale correlation of interfacial structure, kinetics, and electrochemical function.</jats:p>
summary: Perspective on applying sub-second HS-AFM to electrochemical interfaces (electrodeposition, dissolution, corrosion, lithiation morphology, nanobubbles). Relevant as an emerging operando nanoscale imaging method, but it is a perspective, broader than batteries, and lithiation is only one topic.

title: Operando Raman Spectroscopy-Guided 24-Hour Aging Assessment of Activated Carbon Positive Electrodes for Lithium-Ion Capacitors
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>While high-power lithium-ion capacitors (LICs) with high energy density emerge as promising pulse-/peak-power solutions for AI data centers, their long-term viability remains severely hindered by the degradation of the activated carbon (AC) positive electrode. To evaluate this aging behavior, we propose a 24-h high-voltage cycling (HVC) protocol integrated with operando Raman spectroscopy, demonstrating that the turning point in the D1 band can serve as a sensitive indicator of corrosion severity. During the early-stage HVC aging, cathode–electrolyte interphase (CEI) formation and gas evolution passivate defect-related Raman signals, narrowing the D1 band. As aging proceeds, carbon corrosion becomes dominant and broadens the D1 band. By validating this approach across various ACs, we establish a direct correlation between an earlier structural turning point and accelerated capacity decay, thereby uncovering carbon aging mechanisms and offering an unprecedented, rapid diagnostic technique for capacitor-type materials.</jats:p>
summary: Uses operando Raman during a 24-h high-voltage cycling protocol on activated carbon cathodes. The turning point in D1 band width (narrowing from CEI/gas passivation, then broadening from corrosion) correlates with capacity decay across different ACs. This gives a fast aging diagnostic, though it is bulk Raman rather than spatially resolved.
